Puzzle 19 · 20 of 26

Why are the first thousand calls slow?

Puzzle 5 traced score's bytecode by hand, one instruction at a time. HotSpot starts out doing the same. Measure what that costs, and see how much faster the same method runs once HotSpot has compiled it.

  • Puzzle 17: Where do classes live, and how do they leak?

    Objects live on the heap; a loaded class's metadata lives in metaspace, memory outside the heap, owned by its defining loader. A class is unloaded only together with its loader, once nothing reaches either, so a single kept object from a plugin keeps its class, its loader and every class that loader defined, and repeated reloads fill metaspace until OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace.

The problem

Puzzle 18 said that ART starts by interpreting DEX and compiles hot methods later. HotSpot, the JVM that ran every program in this course, works the same way, and you can measure it. This program calls puzzle 5's score a thousand times per batch and times 200 batches with System.nanoTime(), a clock in nanoseconds:

public class Score {
    static int score(int visits, int stars) {
        int total = visits * 2 + stars;
        return total;
    }

    static int batch(int stars) {
        int sum = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) {
            sum += score(i, stars);
        }
        return sum;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int sum = 0;
        for (int b = 1; b <= 200; b++) {
            long start = System.nanoTime();
            sum += batch(b);
            long nanos = System.nanoTime() - start;
            System.out.println("batch " + b + ": " + nanos + " ns");
        }
        System.out.println(sum);
    }
}

Two runs of java Score, and two with the Xint option, which turns HotSpot's compilers off (only some batches shown; the full output has 200 lines):

Batchdefault, run 1default, run 2Xint, run 1Xint, run 2
318,856 ns15,023 ns18,525 ns19,490 ns
5017,305 ns14,072 ns19,114 ns18,973 ns
802,747 ns13,550 ns18,941 ns18,419 ns
1003,091 ns1,915 ns19,172 ns19,213 ns
200610 ns1,947 ns19,601 ns18,503 ns

The same thousand calls cost about 19,000 nanoseconds (19 per call) at the start of every run, and stayed there with the compilers off. With them on, the cost dropped to about 2,000 nanoseconds or less, at a different batch in each run. What was HotSpot doing during the slow batches, and why does it start that way?

See it

The building block

An interpreter is a program that carries out bytecode one instruction at a time, as puzzle 18 said of ART. Machine code is the processor's own instructions, which run without one (puzzle 5 called them machine instructions).

HotSpot's interpreter is a template interpreter. When HotSpot starts, it generates, for every opcode, a small piece of machine code, the template, that carries out that one instruction. Running score in the interpreter means, for each of its 8 instructions: read the opcode at the current offset, jump to that opcode's template, let the template work on the frame's local slots and operand stack (puzzles 1 and 5), then read the next opcode. OpenJDK's runtime overview says it in its own words: HotSpot "generates an interpreter in memory at the startup", from "assembly code corresponding to each bytecode".

That is faster than a loop that compares the opcode against every case, but it still pays for every instruction: the read, the jump, and passing each value through the operand stack in the frame. Compiled code for score does the work of all 8 instructions without reading a single opcode or jumping between templates. That gap is what the table above measures: about 19 nanoseconds per call interpreted, about 2 or less compiled, in these runs on this machine.

So why not compile everything before main starts? Because most code runs rarely. The runtime overview: "Virtually all programs spend the vast majority of their time executing a minority of their code." Compiling a method takes time and memory, and for a method that runs a few times the interpreter finishes first. So HotSpot "immediately runs the program using an interpreter, and analyzes the code as it runs to detect the critical hot spots in the program". To find them, it keeps an invocation counter for every method, increased on each call. When a method's count crosses a threshold, HotSpot hands it to a compiler, a JIT (just-in-time) compiler because it compiles while the program runs. The machine code goes into the code cache, memory outside the heap reserved for compiled code (240 megabytes at most, by default).

That explains the slow batches. Compiling happens in the background, on separate compiler threads: the java manual says "the JVM compiles the method as a background task, running the method in interpreter mode until the background compilation is finished." The calls during the first batches ran in the interpreter while counters climbed and compilers worked; the drop came when compiled code arrived. Why it came at batch 80 in one run and batch 100 in the other, and why compiling score alone wasn't enough, is puzzle 20's subject.

The edges

  • Interpreted, not slow everywhere. 19 nanoseconds a call is fast for a request that runs once. The cost matters only for code that runs many times, and that's exactly the code HotSpot compiles.
  • Xint is for experiments. With it, the java manual says, "all bytecode is executed by the interpreter". Nothing in production should run like that. The default, interpret first and compile hot methods, is what the manual calls mixed mode, and java -version prints it: "mixed mode".
  • Android does it too. ART interprets DEX, compiles hot methods while the app runs, and dex2oat compiles profiled methods ahead of time (puzzle 18).
  • Numbers depend on the machine. The nanoseconds above come from one Linux machine running OpenJDK 21; yours will differ. The ratio, interpreted several times slower than compiled, is what carries over.

The analogy

A clerk handles each request by looking up every line of the procedure in the office manual before doing it: find the page for "add", do it, find the page for "multiply", do it. It's reliable, and it works for a request seen once. The clerk also keeps a tally of how often each kind of request comes in. When one kind passes a few hundred, a specialist writes it out as a single sheet the clerk can follow without opening the manual.

Run it yourself

Save the program above as Score.java, then:

javac Score.java
java Score | head -5
java Score | tail -3
java -Xint Score | tail -3

Before running, predict batch 200 in both modes. Run each twice: the batch where the default run speeds up moves.

Check yourself

You run the 200 batches with the Xint option and print batch 1,000 instead of 200. What does it cost?

Not quite. The interpreter does the same work per instruction on every call; only compiled code is faster.

Right. Xint turns the compilers off for the whole run.

Not quite. The counter only decides when to compile; with Xint it decides nothing.

Why doesn't HotSpot compile every method before main starts?

Right. "A minority of their code" does most of the work.

Not quite. The code cache holds up to 240 megabytes of compiled code from any class.

Not quite. HotSpot chooses to wait for counts; nothing forces it to. Re-read that part ↑

Your server's first request calls 300 methods that never ran before, in classes not used yet. Which costs does that request pay?

Not quite. Methods start in the interpreter and are compiled only once they are hot.

Right. A first request meets both lazy loading and the interpreter.

Not quite. Puzzle 11: a class is loaded the first time code needs it, not at startup. Re-read that part ↑

Sources
  • OpenJDK: HotSpot Runtime Overview, Interpreter ("The current HotSpot interpreter, which is used for executing bytecodes, is a template based interpreter. The HotSpot runtime a.k.a. InterpreterGenerator generates an interpreter in memory at the startup using the information in the TemplateTable (assembly code corresponding to each bytecode). A template is a description of each bytecode."; "The template design performs better than a classic switch-statement loop"; "Virtually all programs spend the vast majority of their time executing a minority of their code. Rather than compiling method by method, just in time, the Java HotSpot VM immediately runs the program using an interpreter, and analyzes the code as it runs to detect the critical hot spots in the program.")
  • The java command (JDK 21) ("-Xint Runs the application in interpreted-only mode. Compilation to native code is disabled, and all bytecode is executed by the interpreter. The performance benefits offered by the just-in-time (JIT) compiler aren't present in this mode."; "-Xmixed Executes all bytecode by the interpreter except for hot methods, which are compiled to native code. On by default."; "-Xbatch Disables background compilation. By default, the JVM compiles the method as a background task, running the method in interpreter mode until the background compilation is finished."; "-XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize= size Sets the maximum code cache size (in bytes) for JIT-compiled code."; "The default maximum code cache size is 240 MB")
  • OpenJDK source, compilationPolicy.hpp, jdk-21+35 (lines 36–37: "The system supports 5 execution levels: * level 0 - interpreter")
  • The timings (four runs, two with -Xint) were produced in this session with OpenJDK 21.0.12 on Linux x86-64.

What you now know

HotSpot starts every method in its template interpreter, which jumps to a small piece of machine code for each bytecode instruction, about ten times slower in this run than compiled code. It counts calls with an invocation counter and compiles only the methods that turn out to be hot, so the first calls of every method are slow by design.
